title: Psychiatric Emergency Language Access: Interpreter Guide for ED Teams
summary: A practical psychiatric emergency interpreter guide for ED teams covering suicide risk, mental status exams, psychosis, de-escalation, and discharge.
body_markdown:
###


Psychiatric assessment depends heavily on the patient's words and speech pattern. Suicide risk, hallucinations, thought disorder, insight, and capacity can be misread when the patient cannot communicate in the language that feels most natural.


###


The interpreter should preserve fragmentation, repetition, uncertainty, and unusual phrasing as closely as possible. The goal is to carry the patient's speech to the clinician without cleaning it up or making a psychiatric judgment.


###


Use language support during triage, suicide and violence risk assessment, the mental status exam, medication discussions, verbal de-escalation, collateral history, disposition, safety planning, and discharge.


###


Yes. AI interpretation can support routine and complex psychiatric emergency conversations when appropriate clinical quality controls are in place. Teams should test fragmented speech, rapid speech, slang, repetition, accents, code-switching, and low-confidence behavior before deployment.


###


Track time to active interpretation, interpreted suicide-risk assessments, interpreted mental status exams, language support during de-escalation and collateral calls, preferred-language discharge materials, return visits, and language-related safety events.
